request: Nous aimerions planifier les visites de maintenance chez nos clients, avec une tournée par technicien et une replanification quand un client annule au dernier moment.

problem.value: Planifier les visites de maintenance chez les clients, organiser une tournée par technicien et replanifier quand un client annule au dernier moment. Le besoin réel (gain de temps de planification, réduction des kilomètres, respect des engagements contractuels de maintenance, taux d'occupation des techniciens) n'est pas formulé.
problem.evidence: « planifier les visites de maintenance chez nos clients, avec une tournée par technicien et une replanification quand un client annule au dernier moment »

current_process.value: Inconnu : on ne sait pas comment les visites sont planifiées aujourd'hui (Excel, agenda, outil existant, à la main par un planificateur) ni comment les annulations sont gérées.

existing_solutions.value: Inconnu : aucun outil existant, déjà licencié ou achetable (logiciel de planification d'interventions / field service, module de GMAO, fonction non activée de la plateforme) n'est mentionné, ni de budget.

success_metrics.value: Inconnu : pas de critère de réussite (temps de replanification, km parcourus, visites réalisées dans les délais contractuels, créneaux annulés re-remplis).

payer.value: Outil interne ou module de la plateforme pour les propres clients de l'entreprise : le commanditaire est le payeur, pas de modèle de revenu à définir.
payer.evidence: « nos clients », « nos techniciens » suggèrent un usage interne

actors.value: Techniciens (exécutent les tournées), un planificateur / responsable d'exploitation (probable), clients (annulent, éventuellement via un contact). Qui crée les visites, qui valide la replanification, qui est prévenu : non précisé.
actors.evidence: « une tournée par technicien », « un client annule »

business_objects.value: Visite de maintenance, Technicien, Client (et site / adresse d'intervention), Tournée (technicien × jour), Annulation. Probablement liées à un contrat de maintenance ; les champs (durée, compétences requises, créneau, adresse) sont à confirmer.
business_objects.evidence: Déduit de la demande ; contexte plateforme (Client, Contact, Contract, Mission)

business_rules.value: Inconnu : critères de constitution d'une tournée (zone géographique, compétences / habilitations, durée des visites, horaires et fenêtres d'accès clients, temps de trajet, charge max), définition de « dernier moment » (délai), règles de replanification (qui est déplacé, priorité contractuelle, pénalités), variation par client ou contrat.

workflow.value: Cycle de vie de la visite non défini (à planifier → planifiée → confirmée → réalisée / annulée / replanifiée). L'origine des visites (échéances de contrat récurrentes, demande client, création manuelle) est inconnue, ainsi que la fin de cycle (compte rendu, facturation).
workflow.evidence: « planifier les visites », « replanification quand un client annule »

integrations.value: Inconnu : notification du technicien et du client lors d'un changement, agenda, cartographie / calcul d'itinéraire, GPS, application mobile, lien avec contrats et facturation de la plateforme.

permissions.value: Hypothèse : un technicien ne voit que sa tournée, le planificateur voit et modifie toutes les tournées. À confirmer, notamment qui peut déplacer une visite d'un autre technicien.
permissions.evidence: Déduit ; contexte plateforme (permissions oubliées jusqu'à la recette)

config_vs_custom.value: Inconnu : règles de planification identiques pour tous les clients/contrats ou spécifiques (fenêtres, délais d'annulation, priorités).

constraints.value: Inconnu : échéance, volume (nombre de techniciens, de visites par jour), contraintes réglementaires (temps de travail, RGPD sur adresses et données clients), dépendances.

edge_cases.value: À traiter : annulation le jour même alors que le technicien est déjà en route, technicien absent, plusieurs annulations simultanées, client qui annule puis rappelle, visite contractuellement obligatoire à ne pas décaler, créneau libéré à remplir ou non, double replanification.
edge_cases.evidence: Déduit de « annule au dernier moment »

reporting.value: Inconnu : suivi des annulations, historique des changements, export. Aucune obligation d'audit ou de conformité n'est mentionnée à ce stade.

acceptance.value: Inconnu : scénarios de recette (ex. : une annulation la veille produit une tournée recalculée et les personnes concernées sont prévenues).

risks.value: Risques à confirmer : adoption par les techniciens sur le terrain, qualité des adresses et durées de visite, tournées recalculées non réalistes, déploiement progressif vs bascule unique.

acquisition.value: Déploiement auprès d'un ensemble connu d'utilisateurs internes (planificateurs, techniciens) : relève du déploiement (risques), pas de l'acquisition.

questions.q: Comment planifiez-vous les visites et gérez-vous les annulations aujourd'hui (Excel, agenda, un outil de planification déjà payé ou envisagé), et avez-vous un budget ou écarté des solutions du marché ?
questions.why: Incertitude élevée × impact élevé : acheter ou activer un outil existant peut supprimer tout ou partie du développement, et le budget dimensionne le reste.

questions.q: D'où viennent les visites à planifier : sont-elles générées automatiquement par les contrats de maintenance (périodicité, échéances à respecter), demandées par les clients, ou saisies à la main ? Et qui les crée et les attribue aux techniciens ?
questions.why: L'origine des visites est le point amont qui peut transformer l'outil en un sous-système complet (contrats, périodicité, demandes) ; elle change fortement le périmètre.

questions.q: Quelles règles doivent respecter une tournée (zone, compétences ou habilitations, durée des visites, horaires d'accès chez le client, temps de trajet, charge maximale par jour) et ces règles varient-elles selon les clients ou les contrats ?
questions.why: Ce sont ces règles qui décident si l'on construit un simple calendrier ou un moteur d'optimisation de tournées.

questions.q: Qu'entendez-vous par « dernier moment » (veille, matin même, technicien déjà en route) et que doit-il se passer alors : la visite est-elle décalée automatiquement ou proposée au planificateur ? Le créneau libéré est-il comblé par une autre visite ? Qui est prévenu (technicien, client, quel contact) ?
questions.why: Le comportement attendu à l'annulation (automatique ou validé par un humain, notifications) change la conception de la replanification et les règles de notification.

questions.q: Combien de techniciens et de visites par jour sont concernés, et qui utilisera l'outil (planificateur au bureau, techniciens sur mobile) ? Une échéance est-elle fixée ?
questions.why: Le volume et les profils d'utilisateurs déterminent l'effort (mobile ou non, calcul de tournée) et les permissions à prévoir.

summary.scope: Probable : création et affectation des visites, constitution des tournées par technicien et par jour, gestion des annulations avec replanification et notification. briefs.problem: Maintenance visits at client sites are planned without a defined way to build each technician's route or to absorb late client cancellations, so the real need (less planning time, fewer kilometres, contractual visit deadlines met) is not yet stated.
briefs.solution: A visit-planning tool that assigns maintenance visits to technicians, builds a daily route per technician, and proposes or applies a rescheduling when a client cancels late (proposed scope, to be confirmed).
introduces: a route-building capability (technician × day) driven by zone, skills and visit duration
a rescheduling engine reacting to a cancellation event, with an automatic or planner-validated mode
a visit lifecycle (to plan, planned, confirmed, done, cancelled, rescheduled) with its own history
role-based notifications to technicians and client contacts on every change
possibly a link to maintenance contracts to generate recurring visits and protect contractual deadlines

challenges.headline: Build versus buy a field-service tool
challenges.premise: A custom planning and routing feature must be built, although the request names no analysis of existing tools.
challenges.alternative: Route planning with rescheduling is a standard problem for field-service scheduling and maintenance-management software. Activating a feature already licensed, or buying such a tool, could cover the need without a build. A build then only covers what is specific, such as the link with our own contracts.
challenges.consequence: Building a routing and rescheduling engine can consume most of the budget to reproduce what an existing tool already does, and leaves the team maintaining it.
challenges.recommendation: Before any design, list what is already licensed or in use, shortlist two or three market options, and compare them to the stated needs. Decide to build only for the gap.

challenges.headline: Optimised routes versus a simple calendar
challenges.premise: A route per technician implies computing optimised itineraries.
challenges.alternative: A first version where the planner assigns visits to a technician's day, sees them grouped by zone, and gets an ordered list without optimisation, avoids a routing engine. Optimisation can be added once the real constraints are known.
challenges.consequence: Starting with automatic optimisation requires travel times, skills, visit durations and access windows that are all unknown today. A recalculated route built on poor data will look wrong to technicians and be rejected.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm how many technicians and visits per day are involved, and what the planner does by hand today, to decide whether optimisation is worth it at all.

challenges.headline: Automatic rescheduling on cancellation
challenges.premise: When a client cancels late, the system should reschedule by itself.
challenges.alternative: On cancellation, the system could free the slot, flag the visit and propose options to the planner, who validates. This is a proposal, not something the client asked for, and automatic mode can be added later.
challenges.consequence: Automatic rescheduling can push back a visit that a maintenance contract requires on a given date, move a technician already on the road, or notify clients wrongly, and nobody has defined what 'last minute' means.
challenges.recommendation: Define 'last minute' (the day before, the same morning, technician already on the way) and which visits are contractually non-movable, then choose between planner-validated and automatic rescheduling per case.

complexity_reasons: rescheduling rules that depend on cancellation timing and contract priority
route building under skills, zone and time constraints, if optimisation is in scope
notifications routed by role to technicians and client contacts
scope still open: from a simple calendar to a full planning engine
briefs.cost_driver: the scope of route building and rescheduling (simple calendar or optimisation engine)
risks: Building something that an already-licensed or purchasable tool would have covered, because no one has checked.
Rescheduling that breaks contractual maintenance deadlines if contract priority is not modelled.
Technicians' adoption in the field: a route changed at the last minute that is unrealistic or poorly communicated will be ignored.
Poor quality of addresses, visit durations and skills data, which makes any computed route unreliable.
Permissions (who can move another technician's visit) discovered late, at acceptance testing.

opportunities.text: Generate maintenance visits from contract schedules so that planning starts from contractual due dates, and make cancellation and rescheduling a reusable event other modules can subscribe to.
Reuse the contact roles (billing, HR, operational) already in the client directory to route cancellation and rescheduling notifications to the right person.
Link a completed visit to final invoicing, as is done for the end of a mission, once planning is stable.

next_steps: Run the build-or-buy check first: inventory tools already licensed or in use, shortlist market options and compare them to the need.
Interview the planner and observe the current process, including how a late cancellation is handled today, to turn the request into measurable goals (planning time, kilometres, deadlines met).

briefs.solution: An internal planning tool that assigns maintenance visits to a daily route per technician and handles late-cancellation re-planning, with the degree of automation still to be decided.

challenges.headline: Build before checking existing tools
challenges.premise: A custom route-planning feature is the right answer to this need.
challenges.alternative: Field-service or route-planning tools, or an unused feature of a tool already licensed, may already cover per-technician routes and cancellation re-planning. Reusing one could shrink the build to an integration with the contract and client directory.
challenges.consequence: Building a scheduling engine from scratch may duplicate something already paid for, and cost far more than the real need justifies.
challenges.recommendation: Before any estimate, inventory current tools and licences and review two or three market options against the stated need and budget.

challenges.headline: Automatic re-planning assumed
challenges.premise: A late cancellation should trigger re-planning of the visit and the route, with the level of automation left implicit.
challenges.alternative: Assisted re-planning is a lower-risk first step: the system proposes slots and a planner validates. It avoids committing to a fully automatic engine before the rules (cut-off delay, same technician, contract priority) are known.
challenges.consequence: Full automation without agreed rules can move visits clients did not accept, break contractual commitments, and requires a much heavier engine.
challenges.recommendation: Define 'last minute' and the re-planning rules with the planners, then start with proposal plus human validation.

challenges.headline: Route optimisation may not be needed
challenges.premise: 'A route per technician' implies optimised routes.
challenges.alternative: A day list ordered by the planner, with visits grouped by zone and skill, delivers most of the value. Automatic optimisation can be added later if volumes justify it.
challenges.consequence: Automatic route optimisation with skills, time windows and start points is an order of magnitude more work than manual ordering, and the volumes are unknown.
challenges.recommendation: Get the number of technicians and visits per day, then decide between manual ordering and optimisation.

briefs.problem: Maintenance visits at customer sites are planned without a stated, reliable way to organise each technician's day and to refill the slot when a customer cancels late; the exact pain (wasted travel, lost slots, missed commitments) has not been given.
briefs.solution: A visit-planning capability that assigns maintenance visits to technicians, orders them into a daily route per technician, and handles a late customer cancellation by rescheduling the visit and notifying the people concerned.
introduces: a visit lifecycle (planned, confirmed, in progress, done, cancelled, rescheduled) with its own state transitions
a daily route per technician, as an ordered set of visits that must be rebuilt when one changes
a late-cancellation and rescheduling flow that frees a slot and proposes or applies a replacement
role-based notifications to technician, customer contact and planner
technician-scoped views and permissions (own route versus all routes)
possibly a route-optimisation component, if automatic itinerary calculation is required

challenges.headline: Build versus buy planning tool
challenges.premise: The request is phrased as something to build, with no mention of any scheduling or field-service tool already in place, already licensed, or evaluated.
challenges.alternative: Assignment of visits to technicians, daily routes and cancellation-driven rescheduling is a self-contained scheduling problem. Reusing an existing module or buying a scheduling tool may cover most of it, leaving only the link to contracts and customers to build.
challenges.consequence: Building a scheduling system from scratch can cost far more than the problem warrants, and could duplicate a feature the company already pays for but has not switched on.
challenges.recommendation: Before any design, inventory what the company already uses or licenses for planning and shortlist two or three off-the-shelf options with a rough budget. Build only the gap.

challenges.headline: Optimised route or ordered list?
challenges.premise: The wording 'a route per technician' is taken to be the same thing whether a planner orders stops by hand or the system calculates the best itinerary.
challenges.alternative: A planner-ordered list of the day's visits, with a map or distance hint, is a small build. Automatic optimisation under customer time windows, technician skills and working-hour limits is a subsystem of its own. Starting with the ordered list lets real data show whether optimisation is worth funding.
challenges.consequence: If optimisation is assumed by default, it dominates cost and schedule, and it must be re-run on every late cancellation, which makes rescheduling more complex.
challenges.recommendation: Ask the client which one they mean, and with what volume (technicians, visits per day, area), before estimating. Treat automatic optimisation as a separate, later decision.

challenges.headline: Automatic rescheduling on cancellation
challenges.premise: A late cancellation is assumed to trigger a rescheduling that the system can simply carry out.
challenges.alternative: Cancellation could free the slot and propose options to a planner (reschedule, fill with another visit, or leave empty) rather than decide alone. The right behaviour depends on how 'late' is defined, whether the visit is contractually due, and whether the cancellation is billable.
challenges.consequence: Automatic rescheduling can breach contractual maintenance commitments, double-book technicians, or notify customers and technicians of changes nobody validated. Retrying or repeating a cancellation could also create duplicate visits.
challenges.recommendation: Define the lateness threshold, the decision-maker and the contractual consequences with the client first. Start with a planner-confirmed proposal, and automate only the cases that prove predictable.

complexity_reasons: visit and route lifecycle where one cancellation ripples into the technician's whole day

notification routing by role and channel
complexity could jump to high if automatic route optimisation or generation of visits from contracts is in scope
briefs.cost_driver: whether routes are optimised automatically or ordered by a planner
risks: Scope creep: the request can silently grow into a full field-service planning system if optimisation and automatic visit generation from contracts are included.
A late cancellation changes a technician's route after it has been communicated, so notifications, concurrent edits and repeated changes to the same visit need clear rules.
Rescheduling rules unknown today (lateness threshold, who decides, billing of late cancellations) could be contractual and vary by customer.
Customer addresses or contact roles may be incomplete in the existing directory, which undermines route ordering and notification routing.
Technician adoption in the field is uncertain: a route view that is hard to use on a phone, or that changes unexpectedly, will be bypassed.

opportunities.text: Treat the visit and its cancel-and-reschedule lifecycle as a reusable scheduling core (states, slot release, notification on change), so it can serve other appointment-like work later.
Route notifications on the operational role already held by each customer contact, so the right person is told about a cancellation or move without new contact data.
Generate expected maintenance visits from recurring maintenance contracts, once the manual planning flow is proven.

Settle the route scope (planner-ordered versus optimised) together with volumes: number of technicians, visits per day, geographic area.
If building, deliver a first slice: visit lifecycle, assignment, an ordered daily route per technician, and cancellation with planner-confirmed rescheduling and role-based notifications.
